sampling_model.design: Before outcomes are observed, the designer chooses any outcome-independent probability law on \(\mathcal A_K^n\), including laws with dependent assignments. The explicit attaining design assigns independently with \(q_a^\star=|c_a|/2\) on the active arms.
sampling_model.units: The population consists of \(n\) fixed labeled units. Each unit has a fixed binary potential outcome under every arm, and the only randomness in risk is assignment and optional estimator randomization.
sampling_model.treatment: Exactly one label in \(\mathcal A_K\) is assigned to each unit; the estimator observes the full assignment vector and the realized binary outcomes.
sampling_model.overlap: The unrestricted game imposes no overlap restriction. The proposed lower bound explicitly covers every allocation-count face, including a zero count for one or more active arms and assignments to inactive arms.
sampling_model.nuisance_estimation: There is no superpopulation nuisance estimation. The nonlinear upper rule uses the finite response-alphabet dual score, and the lower bound uses a finite-schedule prior localized along the target direction and all contrast-orthogonal directions.

comparator_promise_table.comparator_claim: The unrestricted binary two-arm minimax risk is \(n^{-1}-C_An^{-4/3}+o(n^{-4/3})\), attained by Bernoulli randomization and nonlinear shrinkage.
For bounded two-arm potential outcomes, independent assignment remains minimax when measurable estimators are unrestricted.

Theorem 2.1 gives permutation symmetrization and complete-randomization content, Theorem 3.1 reduces the minimax problem over linear-estimator schemes to minimization of a quadratic expected form subject to linear constraints over assignment and estimator schemes, and Theorem 3.2 gives the two-arm complete-randomization, Neyman-allocation, and difference-in-means specialization.

For two-arm controlled experiments, complete randomization is minimax for effect-estimation precision under a permutation-symmetric conditional-mean class, and inference-constrained mixed strategies optimize precision subject to design-uniformity constraints.
Under unbiased estimation of bounded finite-population totals, pairwise-independent sampling attains a sharp minimax bound.
Second-order minimax optimality can be characterized through positive solutions of a problem-specific Schrodinger equation.
Design-based estimators and variance adjustments are developed for pairwise contrasts in multi-armed randomized trials.
Adaptive treatment assignments are optimized for final multi-arm Stein-like shrinkage estimators by evaluating heteroscedastic Gaussian shrinkage risk.

body.tldr: On the explicit union of the published normalized two-arm class and the new class of fixed normalized binary contrasts with at least three active arms, the unrestricted finite-population design-estimation game has a universal Airy correction whose contrast dependence is exactly the finite response-alphabet gauge \(V_c(s_c/2)\). Contrast-weighted independent assignment and a total full-label nonlinear estimator attain the coefficient on the new component, while the two-arm reduction bridges to the published component. A full-dimensional piecewise-polynomial finite-schedule prior must establish the matching lower bound uniformly over dependent designs and every zero-count face. For rational contrasts, a terminating algorithm returns a finite proof-checkable certificate record and a total evaluator that generates exact risk brackets at each requested future sample size; rational bracketing transfers the mathematical expansion, but not Turing evaluation, to arbitrary real contrasts.

project_justification.gap: Sudijono, Dobriban, and Tchetgen Tchetgen (2026), Theorems 2.2 and 3.1, solve the unrestricted binary two-arm game through a scalar ancillary experiment and an Airy least-favorable prior. Hull (2026), Theorem 1, independently reduces the bounded two-arm game. Neither construction handles a signed contrast with a multidimensional nuisance kernel, a response alphabet of size \(2^{|S_c|}\), or allocation faces that omit an active arm.
project_justification.niche: The response-alphabet gauge isolates the contrast-specific cusp while a basis consisting of the target direction and \(\ker(c^\top)\) supplies target-changing directions invisible on every missing-arm face. This geometry can support a single prior whose conditional Bayes risk is uniform over every realized count vector and hence every dependent outcome-independent design.
project_justification.fill: The paper will prove the Airy headline on the explicit union of the published normalized two-arm class and the new at-least-three-active-arm class, with the two-arm reduction as the bridge; identify \(C_AV_c(s_c/2)^{2/3}\); construct the explicit independent design and nonlinear estimator on the new component; and provide a finite proof-checkable certificate record with a total exact per-sample-size evaluator for rational inputs. The central open content is the exact-target weak integration-by-parts inequality and its uniform local, exterior, inactive-arm, and zero-count remainder control.

body.related_work: Sudijono, Dobriban, and Tchetgen Tchetgen (2026), Theorems 2.1--2.3 and 3.1 and Appendix C, provide the writing and estimation exemplars: a finite scalar reduction, nonlinear Airy shrinkage, and discretized least-favorable priors for two arms. Hull (2026), Theorem 1 and its three-step symmetrization proof, shows that bounded outcomes can favor independent assignment even with arbitrary measurable estimators, but remains two-arm. Bai (2023), Theorem 2.1, establishes permutation symmetrization and the associated complete-randomization content; Theorem 3.1 reduces the minimax problem over linear-estimator schemes to minimization of a quadratic expected form subject to linear constraints over assignment and estimator schemes; and Theorem 3.2 gives the two-arm complete-randomization, Neyman-allocation, and difference-in-means specialization. Those restrictions do not settle the present fixed-schedule nonlinear game. Kallus (2021) studies minimax precision in two-arm controlled experiments over a conditional-mean class with a minimax-variance objective, proving complete randomization under permutation symmetry and constructing inference-constrained mixed-strategy designs; its objective and admissible design class differ from worst-schedule squared risk over binary potential outcomes with arbitrary outcome-independent assignments and unrestricted labeled-data estimators. Aronow and Lopatto (2026), Theorems 2 and 3, retain exact finite arithmetic for bounded totals but impose unbiasedness. Levit (1986) supplies the positive-eigenfunction architecture linking second-order minimax risk and a Schrodinger ground state. Rosenman and Hunter (2026) optimize sequential adaptive assignments for final multi-arm Stein-like shrinkage estimators by evaluating heteroscedastic Gaussian shrinkage risk; that adaptive Gaussian decision problem is distinct from minimax risk over fixed binary schedules, arbitrary outcome-independent assignment laws, and unrestricted labeled-data estimators. Schochet (2018) supplies conventional design-based multi-arm estimators but does not motivate the proposal-specific requirement of at least three active contrast coordinates. Hammer et al. (1996) supplies the four-regimen application rather than a theorem comparator.
body.honest_scope: The new multi-arm theorem is pointwise in every fixed permitted contrast and fixed arm count; the headline is stated on the explicit union with the published normalized two-arm class, connected by the two-arm reduction. It makes no growing-arm or vanishing-weight-uniform claim. The effective theorem accepts rational contrasts and rational tolerances and returns a finite symbolic record containing a total exact evaluator for requested integers beyond its threshold. Its continuity corollary transfers the mathematical coefficient to real contrasts but does not claim computation from an unrepresented real. Weak-null inference, covariate balancing, and interval-valued endpoint reduction are separate follow-on questions. The all-count exact-target Bayes inequality is explicitly open and is not disguised as an assumption.
